hook_text: A finger on a tiny syringe lifts a mass the big syringe could not. The catch is written in millimetres.
clip_script: Small syringe as master, big syringe as slave, water between, no bubbles. Push the small plunger lightly and the big one lifts half a kilo. Your push makes a pressure; the pressure acts on the whole big face; bigger face, bigger force, by the ratio of the areas, about 2.5 for a 5 and a 20. The catch: push 20 millimetres in and the big one rises 8. More force, less travel. Swap them and it flips: the small plunger flies out 20 for 8 pushed in, but with less force. The big face always wins on force and loses on distance. Force times distance stays the same at both ends. That is the jack, the rescue spreader, and every hydraulic machine: multiply one, divide the other.
visual_style: Whiteboard small and large syringe joined by a tube; a mass rising slowly; arrows sized for force and distance swapping as the syringes swap; a force-times-distance equation held constant.
mood: Delighted discovery with an honest catch.
pacing: The surprise lift, the area reason, the distance catch, the swap, the rule.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and measure the diameters of two syringes to predict their ratio.
